concepts.title: What Fine-Tuning Actually Changes
concepts.description: Prompting and RAG change what a frozen model conditions on for a single call; fine-tuning runs gradient descent and permanently rewrites the model's weights, a mechanically different, more powerful, and riskier operation than either.
learningObjectives: Explain, at the level of weight updates, what happens during a fine-tuning training step versus what happens when you add instructions or retrieved text to a prompt.

Distinguish in-context learning (transient, no weight change) from parametric learning via fine-tuning (persistent weight change), and explain why only the latter survives once a conversation or session ends.

Describe the fine-tuning training loop conceptually: loss computed against target completions, gradients computed with respect to every trainable weight, and an optimizer nudging weights to reduce that loss.
Explain catastrophic forgetting and why updating weights to improve one narrow behavior can silently degrade unrelated capabilities.
Predict, given a described training setup, whether a fine-tune is likely to improve a target behavior cleanly or put unrelated capabilities at risk.

sections.heading: In-Context Learning vs Parametric Learning
sections.body:
Every technique from the previous module (a more specific instruction, a few-shot example, a retrieved document) works by changing what gets fed into a model whose weights never move. The model reads a different sequence of tokens on each call, its internal activations shift for that one forward pass, and the output changes, but the numbers stored in its weight matrices are the same before and after the call. This is usually called **in-context learning**: the model appears to 'learn' from the examples or instructions in the prompt, but that is a property of conditioning a fixed, frozen function on a particular input. When the prompt is gone (the next call doesn't include it, the session ends, someone forgets to pass the system message), the effect goes with it, because nothing about the model was touched.

Fine-tuning is a different operation: it is additional training, running the gradient-descent procedure that originally produced the model's weights on a new, smaller, purpose-built dataset. The result is a model whose weight matrices contain different numbers than before, and since the model consults those numbers on every future call, the behavior shift persists with no need to re-supply an instruction or an example. This is the core distinction of the module: prompting and RAG operate on a frozen function's input; fine-tuning operates on the function itself.

sections.heading: What a Fine-Tuning Step Computes
sections.body:
Recall the autoregressive generation loop from the how-LLMs-work module: a forward pass produces one logit per vocabulary entry at each position, softmax converts those into a probability distribution, and a token is selected. A fine-tuning training step reuses that forward-pass machinery, for a different purpose and with extra steps attached.

Given a training example (an input plus a desired target completion), the model runs the forward pass it would for ordinary generation, producing a probability distribution over the vocabulary at every position in the target. Instead of sampling from that distribution, training computes a **loss**: a single number (typically cross-entropy) measuring how far the predicted distribution was from the actual target token at each position, averaged over the example. In most chat fine-tuning setups the loss is computed only on the assistant's target tokens, not on the prompt. A low loss means the model already assigned high probability to the correct target tokens; a high loss means it assigned that probability to something else.

```python
# Conceptual shape of ONE fine-tuning training step (not real framework code)
logits = model.forward(input_tokens)                 # same forward pass as inference
loss = cross_entropy(logits, target_tokens)           # how wrong were the predictions?
loss.backward()                                        # compute d(loss)/d(weight) for EVERY weight
optimizer.step()                                       # nudge every weight slightly to reduce loss
optimizer.zero_grad()                                  # clear gradients before the next example/batch
```

The extra machinery, absent from inference, is `loss.backward()` and `optimizer.step()`. Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every single trainable weight in the model -- a partial derivative answering 'if I nudged this one weight up slightly, would the loss go up or down, and by how much?' -- for every weight, all at once. The optimizer (commonly a variant of Adam) then moves each weight a small step in the direction that reduces the loss. Repeat this over many examples, in batches, across multiple passes (**epochs**) through the dataset, and the accumulated nudges are what 'the model learned something new' means. Nothing here is symbolic or rule-based; it is the same numerical optimization that produced the base model's weights, applied to a small, targeted dataset and starting from an already-trained model instead of from scratch. Because the starting point is already good, fine-tuning typically uses a much smaller learning rate than pretraining did (values around 1e-5 are common for full fine-tuning, and around 1e-4 for LoRA) and only a few epochs. The usual overfitting signal is training loss still falling while loss on held-out examples starts to rise. A small run on a few dozen examples, watched step by step, is a cheap way to check that the loss really does move before you scale up; if it doesn't, suspect the data format or a bug before suspecting the model.

sections.heading: Persistence and Its Cost: Catastrophic Forgetting
sections.body:
Fine-tuning writes new values into weights shared across every capability the model has, not into an isolated task-specific module, so nothing structurally guarantees that improving performance on your narrow data leaves everything else untouched. Every weight the optimizer nudges toward the target behavior also contributed, diffusely, to many other behaviors the base model was good at. Push those weights hard in service of a narrow objective (too high a learning rate, too many epochs, a training set that's small or skewed relative to what the model used to do well) and you can degrade unrelated capabilities, a phenomenon called **catastrophic forgetting**. It is a spectrum, not a switch: light fine-tuning with a modest learning rate usually costs little, which is part of why it stays easy to miss. The usual mitigations follow from the causes: a lower learning rate, fewer epochs, parameter-efficient methods like LoRA (covered next), and mixing a sample of general-purpose examples into the training data so the weights keep getting pushed on the old behavior too.

It is dangerous because it's silent by default: the fine-tuning process raises no error or warning. Training loss on your target dataset will look great, since it's being optimized to go down, while performance on tasks you never tested gets worse, and the only way to notice is to test those tasks before and after. A model fine-tuned intensively on customer-service refund replies might become excellent at refund replies and, invisibly, worse at general reasoning, code help, or other customer-service categories it used to handle. Nobody told it to forget those things; the shared weights that supported them were repeatedly nudged toward a narrower objective.

sections.heading: Keep the Base Model Around, and Evaluate Broadly
sections.body:
Because forgetting is a silent risk rather than a rare edge case, treat a candidate fine-tune like any risky code change: compare it against a baseline on a broad regression suite, not just the metric you were trying to improve. Keep the base (pre-fine-tune) model available as that baseline. A fine-tuned model is base weights plus a set of updates, and having the unmodified original to compare against is what lets you detect forgetting instead of assuming it away.

```python
# A minimal before/after regression check -- not just the target task
baseline_scores = evaluate(base_model, eval_suite)          # covers MANY tasks, not just the target one
candidate_scores = evaluate(finetuned_model, eval_suite)

for task in eval_suite.tasks:
    delta = candidate_scores[task] - baseline_scores[task]
    if task == "target_task" and delta <= 0:
        print(f"WARNING: fine-tune did not improve the task it was meant to improve: {task}")
    if task != "target_task" and delta < -0.05:   # illustrative regression threshold; pick one for your suite
        print(f"WARNING: possible forgetting on unrelated task: {task} (delta={delta:.3f})")
```

Compare the fine-tune against the strongest cheap alternative too, not just the base model: a well-prompted base model, or the base model with retrieval, is what you'd actually ship if the fine-tune weren't worth it. The common mistake is gating deployment purely on whether the fine-tune improved the one metric it was trained for. That check nearly always passes, since training optimized that number, and it says nothing about what regressed alongside it.

examples.title: A Toy Fine-Tuning Step, Made Explicit
examples.code:
import torch

# A single, tiny fine-tuning step in PyTorch style (fragment: assumes `model` and `tokenizer`
# for an encoder-decoder model such as T5 are already loaded).
input_ids = tokenizer("Summarize: The meeting is moved to 3pm.", return_tensors="pt").input_ids
target_ids = tokenizer("The meeting time changed to 3pm.", return_tensors="pt").input_ids

optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-5)

outputs = model(input_ids=input_ids, labels=target_ids)   # forward pass + built-in loss computation
loss = outputs.loss
print("loss before step:", loss.item())

loss.backward()        # gradients for every trainable weight
optimizer.step()       # every weight nudged slightly toward lower loss on THIS example
optimizer.zero_grad()  # reset for the next example

# Running this same input through the model again immediately afterward would
# typically show a LOWER loss -- the weights genuinely changed, even if by a tiny amount.
examples.explanation: This is one step out of what a real run repeats many thousands of times. `model(input_ids=input_ids, labels=target_ids)` runs the forward pass used for ordinary generation, and because `labels` is supplied it also computes cross-entropy loss against the target tokens. `loss.backward()` is where the learning happens: it walks the computational graph backward and computes, for every trainable weight, how much that weight contributed to this loss value. `optimizer.step()` then applies a small nudge to each of those weights. None of this exists in a normal inference call, which runs only the forward pass and reads off a distribution, never computes a loss, never calls `.backward()`, and never touches the optimizer. That's why running inference a thousand times never changes the model, while running this training step a thousand times does. The `labels=target_ids` form fits an encoder-decoder model such as T5; for a decoder-only model you concatenate prompt and target into one sequence, pass it as both `input_ids` and `labels`, and mask the prompt positions so loss is computed only on the target.

examples.title: Same Target Behavior, Two Different Mechanisms, Two Different Failure Modes
examples.explanation: Both functions can produce equally formal replies today. The difference shows up under an ordinary production accident: a code path that builds the messages list without the system prompt, such as a refactor that drops it, a new caller that forgets it, or a fallback path during an outage. Approach A's formality disappears the moment the system message is missing, because the frozen base model has no memory of being asked to be formal outside that input. Approach B is unaffected by that bug, because the behavior isn't stored in a prompt; it's in the weights, which are present on every call. (The two model names are placeholders, and the functions return the raw API response.) That is the practical face of 'in-context learning is transient, fine-tuning is persistent': it determines which classes of bugs can silently break a behavior and which can't.

examples.title: Catastrophic Forgetting Showing Up in an Eval Table
examples.explanation: This is the shape of a fine-tune that overfit a narrow dataset: it was trained heavily (too many epochs, too high a learning rate, or too narrow a dataset relative to the model's prior range) on refund replies, and the refund metric improved substantially, since that is what training optimized. The other three metrics, covering unrelated or loosely related capabilities, all regressed, some severely. (The numbers are made up for illustration; the printed output is `refund_reply_quality: 0.62 -> 0.94 (IMPROVED, delta=+0.32)` and so on.) Training didn't 'choose' to sacrifice general QA or code help; nothing in gradient descent protects capabilities that the current batch isn't reinforcing. A team that measured only `refund_reply_quality` would see an unambiguous win right up until users noticed the model got worse at everything else.

misconceptions.description: Fine-tuning is basically just a way to give the model a permanent, extra-long system prompt so you don't have to keep repeating the same instructions on every call.
misconceptions.clarification: The visible effect can look similar, but the mechanism differs, with real consequences. A system prompt is text the frozen model conditions on for one call; fine-tuning runs gradient descent that changes the numbers in the model's weights. The prompting version costs tokens on every call and vanishes if the prompt is omitted; the fine-tuned version adds no per-call prompt cost and persists with no prompt at all, but carries a risk prompting doesn't: catastrophic forgetting of unrelated capabilities, because the shared weights that encode the new behavior also encode everything else the model does.

misconceptions.description: If a fine-tune measurably improves accuracy on the target task, it's a pure win -- there's no meaningful downside to worry about as long as that one number went up.
misconceptions.clarification: Falling training loss and rising target-task accuracy are what the training process directly optimizes, so they will reliably look good, which tells you nothing about capabilities the training data wasn't reinforcing. Catastrophic forgetting is silent: it raises no error and shows up only if you evaluate a broad regression suite covering tasks unrelated to the fine-tune and compare against the pre-fine-tune baseline. Judging a fine-tune solely by the metric it was trained to improve is a common way teams ship a regression and only hear about it from users.
misconceptions.fact: Falling training loss and rising target-task accuracy are what the training process directly optimizes, so they will reliably look good, which tells you nothing about capabilities the training data wasn't reinforcing.

exercises.prompt: A team fine-tunes a general-purpose assistant model using only examples of refund-request replies, for many epochs, at a relatively high learning rate, and evaluates ONLY on a held-out set of refund-reply examples before deciding to deploy. Predict what an evaluation on unrelated tasks (general Q&A, code help) would most likely show, and explain why, even though nobody trained the model to get worse at those things.
exercises.code:
training_data = load_examples("refund_replies_only.jsonl")   # ~2,000 examples, one narrow category
finetune(base_model="assistant-v2", data=training_data, epochs=8, learning_rate=5e-4)
# deployed after refund_reply_eval_score improved from 0.61 to 0.93
hints: The training data reinforces one narrow behavior, for many epochs, at a fairly aggressive learning rate. What does that combination tend to do to weights that also support OTHER capabilities?

Nothing in gradient descent protects capabilities that the current training batch isn't reinforcing; shared weights get nudged toward whatever the loss currently rewards, whatever else depended on their previous values.
Consider what would actually have to be true for unrelated capabilities to be UNAFFECTED -- would that require something special to have been included in this training run? Was it?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Unrelated task performance (general Q&A, code help) is likely to have regressed, even though nobody trained the model to be worse at them. This is catastrophic forgetting, driven by training on a narrow, single-category dataset for many epochs at a high learning rate, with nothing protecting the weights that supported unrelated capabilities. (How large the regression is can't be known without testing, which is the point.)
exercises.solutionExplanation: Training only on refund replies, for many epochs, at a high learning rate is close to a worst-case recipe for forgetting. Many epochs reinforce the same narrow pattern repeatedly; a high learning rate makes each nudge to the shared weights larger; and a single-category dataset means nothing in the training signal reinforces the model's other capabilities. Since all capabilities live in the same weights, pushing them hard toward one objective degrades unrelated ones as a side effect of optimization, not through any instruction to forget. The team's evaluation couldn't reveal this, because it measured only the metric training was already optimizing. A broad regression suite covering unrelated tasks, run before and after, is what catches this kind of damage before production.

exercises.prompt: This deployment gate is meant to prevent bad fine-tunes from reaching production automatically, but after several fine-tuning rounds, users start reporting the assistant has gotten noticeably worse at tasks unrelated to what was being improved. Find the bug in the gating logic and fix it.
hints: This function only looks at one key, "target_task", out of what are presumably several keys in both score dictionaries. What happens to every OTHER task's score, good or bad?
A fine-tune that improves the target task while regressing several unrelated tasks would make this function return True every time. Is that the policy the team wants?
Fix it so deployment also requires that no unrelated task has regressed beyond some acceptable tolerance, not just that the target task improved.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original gate checks one number, whether the target task improved, and ignores every other entry in the score dicts, even though they hold scores for other tasks. A narrow fine-tune reliably improves its own target metric while sometimes regressing unrelated ones, so this gate approves exactly the kind of fine-tune that caused the reported problem. The fix keeps the target-improvement requirement and adds a second: loop over every other task and block deployment if any regressed by more than a chosen tolerance relative to the baseline. This doesn't eliminate forgetting, but it stops a forgetting-heavy fine-tune from being auto-approved because its own metric looked good. The 0.03 tolerance is illustrative; with noisy evals, pick it relative to the measurement noise.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes what fine-tuning changes from what prompting and RAG change?
options: Fine-tuning runs gradient descent that updates the model's weights, persisting after the training run ends; prompting and RAG leave the weights untouched and only change what a frozen model conditions on for one specific call.
Fine-tuning only changes the default system prompt that gets prepended to every call; prompting and RAG change the model's weights.
RAG updates the model's weights to memorize retrieved documents, while fine-tuning and prompting only affect the current call.
There is no real difference -- all three are different ways of writing instructions the model reads before responding.
assessments.explanation: Fine-tuning is additional training: it computes gradients and updates weights via an optimizer, and the updated weights persist across every future call. Prompting and RAG never touch the weights; they change the input a frozen model conditions on for one call, and the effect vanishes when that input isn't included. The “Fine-tuning only changes the default system prompt…” and “RAG updates the model's weights to memorize…” options both invert which technique changes weights. The “There is no real difference -- all…” option collapses a real mechanical distinction (persistent weight updates versus per-call conditioning) into 'it's all just instructions,' the misconception this concept corrects.

assessments.prompt: A senior engineer proposes: 'We don't need a retrieval system anymore -- let's just fine-tune the model on a fresh snapshot of our documentation every week, so it always knows the latest information.' Explain, mechanically, why weekly fine-tuning is a different (and riskier) way to keep a model current than a retrieval system that leaves weights frozen, and identify a specific risk beyond staleness that this weekly-retraining plan introduces.
assessments.modelAnswer: A retrieval system never touches the model's weights: the generation model stays frozen and only the text included in the prompt changes, by searching an index that can be updated in minutes whenever the documentation changes. Fine-tuning is a different operation: it runs gradient descent, computing a loss against target completions and nudging every trainable weight, which is slow, expensive, and changes the model itself rather than its input. Doing that weekly doesn't just inherit the usual problems of fine-tuning for knowledge (weights encode facts diffusely, so even a fresh fine-tune isn't an exact lookup the way injected retrieved text is); it compounds a second risk across every cycle: catastrophic forgetting. Each run nudges shared weights toward that week's snapshot, with no guarantee that every previously learned capability, including whatever the previous week's fine-tune reinforced, stays intact. Run weekly for months, that is months of accumulated, uncontrolled weight drift with no point where anyone verified an earlier capability hasn't degraded. A retrieval index, by contrast, can be corrected, rolled back, or inspected for exactly what text it will inject, with no risk to the model's other behaviors, because the model never changes.

assessments.prompt: During an ordinary inference call to a model, which of the operations involved in a fine-tuning training step are actually performed?
options: The forward pass, loss computation, and backward pass all run, but the optimizer step is skipped to save time.
All four steps -- forward pass, loss computation, backward pass, and optimizer step -- run on every inference call, just using a very small learning rate.
Only the forward pass -- logits are computed and a token is selected from the resulting distribution; no loss is computed.
The forward pass and loss computation both run, but the backward pass and optimizer step are skipped.
assessments.explanation: Inference runs only the forward pass and reads off a probability distribution to select a token from. There is no target completion to compute a loss against, so nothing like `loss.backward()` or `optimizer.step()` executes, which is why running inference many times never changes the model's weights. The “The forward pass and loss computation both…”, “The forward pass, loss computation, and backward…”, and “All four steps -- forward pass, loss…” options all assume some training machinery runs during ordinary inference, when none does; loss computation, gradients, and optimizer updates belong only to a training step.

assessments.prompt: Per this module, why is catastrophic forgetting described as 'silent by default'?
options: Because forgetting only ever happens during the very first epoch of training, before most logging frameworks are typically initialized.
Because it only ever affects models that are deployed without any monitoring dashboard configured.
Because catastrophic forgetting always throws a specific, named exception that many teams accidentally catch and silently swallow in their training scripts.
Because training loss on the target dataset keeps looking good -- it's the exact metric being directly optimized.
assessments.explanation: Nothing in the fine-tuning process raises an error or warning when forgetting happens: the target metric will look good because it's what's being optimized, while unrelated capabilities can degrade, detectable only through deliberate evaluation of tasks outside the training objective. The “Because it only ever affects models…”, “Because forgetting only ever happens during…”, and “Because catastrophic forgetting always throws a specific…” options all invent mechanisms or triggers (missing dashboards, first-epoch-only timing, a swallowed exception); the actual reason is that nothing in the training loop checks or reports on capabilities it isn't optimizing.

assessments.prompt: Per this module, what's the specific flaw in gating a fine-tune's deployment purely on whether it improved the one metric it was trained for?
options: The flaw is that target-metric-only gating requires re-running the full training job twice, which needlessly doubles compute cost without any real benefit.
The target metric will reliably look good precisely because the training process was directly optimizing exactly that number.
There's no real flaw -- if the target metric improved, that alone is sufficient evidence the fine-tune is safe to ship.
The flaw is that target-metric evaluation is always less accurate than LLM-as-judge evaluation, regardless of what specific capability is being measured.
assessments.explanation: Gating deployment on the trained-for metric alone will look successful because that's what the optimization targeted, while giving no visibility into what else regressed, which is why a broad regression suite compared against the retained base-model baseline is the better practice. The “There's no real flaw…” option contradicts that warning. The “The flaw is that target-metric evaluation…” option brings in an unrelated and unsupported comparison to LLM-as-judge evaluation. The “The flaw is that target-metric-only gating requires…” option misdiagnoses a measurement blind spot as a compute-cost problem.

concepts.title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and LoRA
concepts.description: Full fine-tuning has to store gradients and optimizer state for every one of a model's parameters; LoRA gets most of the practical benefit by freezing the original weights and training a small low-rank update alongside them, which is also why adapters can be swapped like plug-ins.
learningObjectives: Explain why full fine-tuning of a large model is memory- and compute-intensive independent of how much training data you have, in terms of gradients and optimizer state per parameter.
Explain the core LoRA idea: freezing the original weight matrices and learning a small low-rank update matrix pair alongside them.
Explain what rank controls in LoRA and the practical tradeoff between rank, learning capacity, and resource cost.
Explain why LoRA adapters are small, swappable, and composable in ways full fine-tuned weight copies are not.
Identify when full fine-tuning is still worth its extra cost over a parameter-efficient approach, and when it clearly isn't.

sections.heading: The Memory Wall of Full Fine-Tuning
sections.body:
Running a large model for inference only needs its weights (and, briefly, its activations) in memory. Training needs considerably more, because gradient descent has to remember more than the current weight values. For every trainable parameter, a full fine-tuning run typically needs the weight itself, the gradient of the loss with respect to that weight (computed fresh each step), and, with a modern optimizer like Adam or AdamW, two running-average tensors per parameter (the first and second moment) that the optimizer uses to adapt its step size per parameter.

Added up, full fine-tuning with Adam-family optimizers needs roughly four times the raw parameter memory at minimum (weights, gradients, two optimizer moments), plus activation memory for the forward and backward passes, before you load a single training example. (Mixed-precision training, which keeps extra full-precision copies, can push the multiple higher.) For a model with tens of billions of parameters, that puts full fine-tuning out of reach of anything but multi-GPU infrastructure, whether your dataset is 500 examples or 500,000: the memory cost depends on model size, not dataset size. That is why teams look for a cheaper way to adapt a model than updating every weight.

sections.heading: The Core LoRA Idea: Freeze the Big Matrix, Learn a Small Update
sections.body:
**LoRA** (Low-Rank Adaptation) sidesteps the memory wall with a trick: instead of updating a weight matrix W, LoRA leaves W frozen (no gradients computed for it) and learns a separate additive update expressed as the product of two much smaller matrices. If W has shape (d x k), LoRA introduces a matrix A of shape (d x r) and a matrix B of shape (r x k), where r, the **rank**, is a small number, often between 8 and 64, tiny relative to d and k. Only A and B are trained; the effective weight is `W + (A @ B) * scaling`, but W is exactly what it always was. (The original paper names the factors the other way round, with B as (d x r) and A as (r x k), and initializes one of them to zero so training starts exactly at the base model; the scaling is usually a hyperparameter alpha divided by r. The idea is identical.)

```python
# Conceptual shapes: original weight matrix vs its LoRA adapter
d, k, r = 4096, 4096, 8

full_matrix_params = d * k                      # 16,777,216 trainable params, if fine-tuned fully
lora_params = (d * r) + (r * k)                  # A: 4096x8, B: 8x4096
print(full_matrix_params, lora_params)           # 16,777,216  vs  65,536
print(full_matrix_params / lora_params)          # roughly 256x fewer trainable parameters for this matrix
```

The hypothesis behind this, which has held up well empirically across many models and tasks, is that the *change* a pretrained model needs for a new, comparatively narrow task or style lives in a low-dimensional subspace, even though the full weight space is enormous. You don't need the full expressive power of a (4096 x 4096) update to teach a consistent tone shift or a narrow classification boundary; a much lower-rank update captures most of the useful adaptation at a small fraction of the trainable parameters, and since only A and B need gradients and optimizer state, the memory wall mostly disappears.

sections.heading: Why Rank Matters
sections.body:
Rank (r) is one of the most consequential hyperparameters in a LoRA setup. A **rank too low** for the behavior shift you're asking for can underfit: if the adaptation needs more expressive capacity than a very low-rank product can represent, training plateaus at a worse result than a higher rank would reach, however much data or how many epochs you add. A **rank too high** eats back the advantages LoRA exists to provide: more trainable parameters, more memory and compute, slower training, and, because a large enough rank approximates full fine-tuning, more exposure to the catastrophic-forgetting risk from the previous concept, since a higher-capacity update has more room to overfit the training set at the expense of everything else.

Teams also don't apply LoRA to every weight matrix. It's commonly applied to a subset, often the attention projection matrices, leaving the others frozen, on the empirical finding that adapting a subset already captures most of the behavior shift (many setups also adapt the feed-forward layers when they need more capacity). Both the rank and which layers to adapt are usually chosen by trying a few settings and measuring task performance, not derived from a formula; there's no rank that's right for every task, only one that's enough for the adaptation you're making.

sections.heading: Swappable, Composable Adapters
sections.body:
Because the original weights are never modified, a LoRA run produces something small: the trained A and B matrices for whichever layers were adapted, typically megabytes (up to a few hundred for large ranks or models) rather than the gigabytes of a full weight copy. That matters for serving: a single base model can be loaded once, and many LoRA adapters (one per customer, task, or style) can be kept as small files and swapped in depending on the request, without reloading the large, slow-to-load base model.

```python
# One shared base model, many small swappable adapters
base_model = load_base_model("assistant-70b")

def generate_for_customer(customer_id, prompt, adapter_paths):
    base_model.set_active_adapter(adapter_paths[customer_id])   # loads a small A/B matrix pair
    return base_model.generate(prompt)
```

With full fine-tuning, each variant is a separate copy of every weight in the model, so serving many variants means storing and possibly loading many full-size copies, which is expensive in a way swapping small adapters isn't. That is what makes it feasible to offer many customers their own 'custom' behavior without a separate full model deployment for each. (The sketch below is deliberately simple; real multi-adapter servers can apply different adapters to different requests in the same batch, which a single global 'active adapter' can't do safely under concurrent traffic.)

sections.heading: When Full Fine-Tuning Still Wins
sections.body: LoRA and other parameter-efficient methods are the sensible default given how much cheaper and lower-risk they are, but they don't replace full fine-tuning everywhere. If the capability shift you need is large (new domain behavior far outside what the base model's representations support, rather than a narrower adaptation of skills it mostly has), a low-rank update may lack the capacity to represent the change, however it's tuned, because the assumption that the needed update is low-dimensional stops holding as the shift gets larger. In those cases full fine-tuning, or at the extreme, further pretraining on a large new corpus, is the appropriate if more expensive and riskier tool. The decision process mirrors the fine-tuning-vs-RAG-vs-prompting heuristic: start with the cheapest, lowest-risk option that could plausibly work (here a modest-rank LoRA adapter) and escalate only with evidence that it falls short. Many full fine-tuning APIs from model providers are in practice parameter-efficient under the hood, so check what a given service actually does. Two practical LoRA details are worth knowing. Because the update is additive, you can merge `A @ B` into `W` once training is done, which gives a single ordinary weight matrix with no extra inference cost (at the price of losing easy swapping). And QLoRA keeps the frozen base weights in a quantized, lower-precision format while training the adapter in higher precision, which lowers memory further. When you run it yourself, the main LoRA settings are the rank, a scaling factor (often called alpha), which weight matrices to adapt, and an optional dropout on the adapter; start from a library's defaults and change one at a time while watching your validation metric.

examples.title: Rough Trainable-Parameter Counts: Full Fine-Tuning vs LoRA
examples.code:
def full_finetune_trainable_params(total_model_params):
    return total_model_params   # every weight is trainable

def lora_trainable_params(d, k, r, num_adapted_matrices):
    per_matrix = (d * r) + (r * k)
    return per_matrix * num_adapted_matrices

total_model_params = 7_000_000_000   # a 7B-parameter model
lora_params = lora_trainable_params(d=4096, k=4096, r=16, num_adapted_matrices=64)

print(full_finetune_trainable_params(total_model_params))   # 7,000,000,000
print(lora_params)                                            # 8,388,608
print(total_model_params / lora_params)                       # roughly 834x fewer trainable parameters
examples.explanation: The full fine-tuning figure is trivial: every weight is trainable, so the trainable count is the model's total, with the gradient and optimizer-state memory that implies for all seven billion numbers. The LoRA figure counts only the A and B matrices across the (illustrative) 64 adapted weight matrices at rank 16, roughly 830 times fewer trainable parameters (7,000,000,000 / 8,388,608 is about 834). That gap is why LoRA is often practical on hardware that couldn't hold the optimizer state for full fine-tuning of the same model: the frozen base weights still need to be loaded for the forward pass, but no gradients or optimizer moments are stored for them, only for the small adapters.

examples.title: A LoRA Update as Matrix Math
examples.code:
import numpy as np

# A small, illustrative frozen weight matrix (imagine this is a real, much larger,
# pretrained weight matrix inside a transformer layer)
W = np.random.randn(6, 6)

# LoRA adapter: rank r=2, much smaller than the 6x6 original
r = 2
A = np.random.randn(6, r) * 0.01   # trained
B = np.random.randn(r, 6) * 0.01   # trained
scaling = 1.0

W_effective = W + scaling * (A @ B)   # used at inference; W itself never changes

print("Original W shape:", W.shape)             # (6, 6) -- 36 values, frozen
print("A shape, B shape:", A.shape, B.shape)      # (6, 2), (2, 6) -- 12 + 12 = 24 trainable values
print("A @ B shape:", (A @ B).shape)              # (6, 6) -- matches W's shape, so it can be added directly
examples.explanation: `A @ B` produces a matrix the same shape as `W`, even though `A` and `B` are individually much smaller. That is the mechanical trick behind LoRA: the product of a (d x r) and an (r x k) matrix is always (d x k), so it can be added directly to the full-size matrix it adjusts. `W` is never assigned to or modified here; only `A` and `B` would receive gradients in real training, and `W_effective` combines the frozen original with the trained update. (The random values are only for shapes; the printed shapes are exactly as in the comments. The seed isn't fixed, so values differ per run.) In this toy example the savings look modest (24 vs 36 values), but the ratio grows large at real transformer sizes, as the previous example showed.

examples.title: Swapping Adapters Per Request
examples.explanation: The slow part, loading a 70-billion-parameter base model, happens once, in `__init__`. Each later call swaps in a small adapter file only if the requested customer differs from the active adapter, which is cheap compared with loading another full-size model. The cost that scales with the number of customers is the small adapter swap, not the base-model load, which is paid once however many adapters exist. Note the check against `self._active_adapter_id`; without it, this code risks the bug in the debugging exercise below, where a stale adapter keeps being used for the wrong customer. (`load_base_model`, `load_adapter` and `adapter_registry` are placeholders; libraries such as Hugging Face PEFT provide equivalents. The class isn't safe for concurrent requests, since the active adapter is shared state.)

misconceptions.description: LoRA fine-tunes the whole model, just in a faster, more memory-efficient way.
misconceptions.clarification: LoRA does not train the model's original weight matrices at all; it freezes them and trains only a separate, much smaller pair of low-rank matrices that are added to the frozen weights at inference time. The base model's weights never change during a LoRA run. That is why one base model deployment can serve many adapters interchangeably: the shared, frozen part is identical across all of them, and only the small adapter differs.
misconceptions.fact: LoRA does not train the model's original weight matrices at all -- it freezes them completely and trains only a separate, much smaller pair of low-rank matrices that get added to the frozen weights at inference time.

misconceptions.description: A higher LoRA rank is always strictly better, since it gives the adapter more capacity to learn the target behavior.
misconceptions.clarification: Higher rank does increase capacity, but capacity beyond what the adaptation needs doesn't sit idle: it costs more memory and compute, moves the setup closer to full fine-tuning's forgetting risk, and gives the optimizer more room to overfit the training set's quirks instead of the intended behavior. Since the premise behind LoRA is that most useful adaptations fit a fairly low-rank subspace, an unnecessarily high rank usually buys little extra quality while giving back some of LoRA's advantages.

exercises.prompt: Write two functions: full_param_count(d, k) returning the number of trainable parameters if a (d x k) weight matrix were fully fine-tuned, and lora_param_count(d, k, r) returning the number of trainable parameters for a LoRA adapter of rank r applied to that same matrix. Then write savings_ratio(d, k, r) that returns how many times fewer trainable parameters the LoRA adapter uses compared to full fine-tuning of that matrix.
hints: A fully fine-tuned (d x k) matrix has d * k trainable parameters, one per entry.
A LoRA adapter introduces two matrices: A of shape (d x r) and B of shape (r x k). Its trainable parameter count is the sum of both matrices' sizes.
savings_ratio should divide the two counts you already computed; call the two functions you wrote instead of duplicating the arithmetic.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `full_param_count` is the size of the full matrix, since every entry gets its own gradient and optimizer state under full fine-tuning. `lora_param_count` reflects LoRA's added structure: A contributes d*r trainable values and B contributes r*k, and since A and B are the only trainable parameters for this weight (the d*k matrix stays frozen), their sum is the adapter's trainable-parameter count. `savings_ratio` reuses both functions, which keeps the relationship explicit: it answers 'how many times fewer trainable parameters does LoRA need,' the number that determines how much of the memory wall a given rank avoids.

exercises.prompt: This multi-tenant serving function is supposed to respond to each customer using that customer's own fine-tuned LoRA adapter. Instead, every customer after the first one gets responses generated using the FIRST customer's adapter, regardless of their own customer_id. Find and fix the bug.
hints: The adapter is loaded only once, guarded by the `_adapter_loaded` flag. Which customer_id was active the first time this function ran?
Every call after the first skips the `if` block, since the flag is already True and is never re-checked against the CURRENT customer_id.
The fix needs to track WHICH adapter is currently active, and reload whenever the requested customer differs from that -- not just whether any adapter has EVER been loaded.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original guard, `_adapter_loaded`, is a boolean that records 'has an adapter been loaded at least once,' not 'which customer's adapter is active.' Once the first request sets it to True, every later request, whatever its `customer_id`, skips the loading branch and keeps using the first adapter, so every other customer is served with the wrong customer's fine-tuned behavior. The fix stores `_active_customer` and compares it with the current `customer_id`, reloading when they differ. It's an ordinary shared-mutable-state bug, fixed like any cache that must be invalidated when its key changes.

assessments.prompt: In a LoRA fine-tuning setup, what happens to the model's original weight matrices, and what actually gets trained?
options: The original weight matrices are frozen and never updated; a separate, much smaller pair of low-rank matrices is trained and added to them at inference time.
The original weight matrices are trained normally; LoRA only changes how the tokenizer processes input to save memory.
The original weight matrices are deleted and replaced entirely by the low-rank matrices, which become the new model.
The original weight matrices are trained at a lower numerical precision to save memory; nothing new is added to the model at training or at inference time.
assessments.explanation: LoRA freezes the original weight matrices (no gradients are computed for them, and their values never change) while training a separate additive low-rank update, the product of two small matrices A and B, alongside them. The “The original weight matrices are trained at…” option describes quantization, a different memory-saving technique (QLoRA does combine the two, training LoRA adapters on a quantized frozen base). The “The original weight matrices are trained normally…” option describes full fine-tuning and defeats the purpose of the adapter. The “The original weight matrices are deleted…” option is wrong because the original weights stay intact and are combined with the adapter's output at inference time, which is what lets the same frozen base weights serve many adapters.

assessments.prompt: A teammate asks how a company can offer hundreds of enterprise customers their own 'custom fine-tuned' version of a very large model without provisioning hundreds of full copies of that model in production. Explain how LoRA-based adapters make this feasible, and specifically what does and does not get duplicated per customer.
assessments.modelAnswer: A LoRA fine-tune never modifies the base model's weights; training produces a separate pair of small low-rank matrices (an adapter) for whichever layers were adapted, and adapter files are typically megabytes rather than the many gigabytes of a full copy. What gets duplicated per customer is only that adapter: each customer's fine-tune produces their own small A/B pair, trained on their data. What does NOT get duplicated is the base model: the large, slow-to-load original weights are loaded once by the serving infrastructure and shared across every customer's requests. At request time the system applies whichever customer's adapter matrices to that one shared base model, then a different customer's for the next request. The cost that scales with the number of customers is storing and swapping small adapter files, not storing and loading hundreds of full-size copies, which is what makes offering many customers custom behavior viable.

assessments.prompt: Per this module, why does full fine-tuning with an Adam-family optimizer need roughly four times the raw parameter memory as a bare minimum, even before a single training example is loaded?
options: Because the forward pass must be run four separate times per training example to compute a numerically stable loss estimate.
Because tokenizing text for training requires four times more memory than tokenizing the same text for inference.

Because for every trainable parameter, memory must hold the weight itself, its gradient, and two optimizer moment tensors that Adam-family optimizers use to adapt step size per parameter -- four values per parameter at minimum, before activation memory is even counted.
Because Adam-family optimizers require four separate full copies of the training dataset to be held in memory simultaneously.
assessments.explanation: The weight, its gradient, and two running-average optimizer moments per parameter account for the roughly 4x figure, independent of dataset size or activation memory. The “Because Adam-family optimizers require four separate full…” option misattributes the multiplier to dataset copies, which Adam doesn't store. The “Because the forward pass must be run…” option invents a repeated-forward-pass requirement. The “Because tokenizing text for training requires four…” option applies the multiplier to tokenization, an unrelated step.

assessments.prompt: Per this module, what's the practical risk of choosing a LoRA rank much higher than what the target adaptation actually needs?
options: A higher rank makes the adapter's matrix shapes incompatible with the frozen base model, so it can no longer be added to it at inference time.
A higher rank always causes training to fail outright with an out-of-memory error, regardless of the model or hardware involved.
A higher rank is purely beneficial with no real tradeoff, since LoRA's design guarantees that more capacity can never hurt.

A higher rank increases memory and compute cost, and as it grows large enough to start approximating full fine-tuning, it also increases exposure to the same catastrophic-forgetting risk covered for full fine-tuning -- often without a corresponding gain in quality.
assessments.explanation: Rank beyond what's needed costs more memory and compute, and as it grows large enough to resemble full fine-tuning it inherits more of the forgetting risk, since a higher-capacity update has more room to overfit instead of generalize, often for little extra benefit. The “A higher rank always causes training…” option overstates the consequence as a guaranteed hard failure. The “A higher rank makes the adapter's matrix…” option is wrong: the shape math (A is d x r, B is r x k) works for any rank. The “A higher rank is purely beneficial…” option contradicts the fact that rank is a real tradeoff, not a free lever.

assessments.prompt: Per this module, what specifically makes it operationally feasible to serve many customers their own custom fine-tuned behavior using LoRA, in a way that full fine-tuning would not support as cheaply?
options: LoRA adapters eliminate the need to load the base model at all, so no shared infrastructure is required for any customer.
Only the small adapter (the trained A and B matrices) differs per customer and can be swapped cheaply onto one shared, frozen base model loaded exactly once.
Full fine-tuning and LoRA cost exactly the same to serve at scale; the only feasibility difference between them is in training time, not serving cost.
LoRA adapters automatically merge every customer's behavior into a single blended response, so only one adapter is ever needed regardless of how many customers exist.
assessments.explanation: The large base model is loaded once and shared, and only small adapter files differ per customer and get swapped in cheaply, in contrast to full fine-tuning's separate full-size copy per customer. The “LoRA adapters eliminate the need to load…” option is wrong -- the base model still must be loaded, just once rather than per customer. The “LoRA adapters automatically merge every customer's behavior…” option invents automatic blending; each customer's adapter is kept and applied separately. The “Full fine-tuning and LoRA cost exactly…” option ignores the serving-cost difference that comes from what must be stored and loaded per customer.

concepts.title: Dataset Preparation for Fine-Tuning
concepts.description: A fine-tuning dataset's quality matters more than its raw size, because gradient descent treats every labeled example as equally trustworthy signal: a mislabeled or unrepresentative example doesn't just fail to help, it teaches the model the wrong association with the same confidence as a correct one.
learningObjectives: Explain why a fine-tuning dataset's format needs to exactly mirror the real inference-time request shape, and predict the consequence when it doesn't.
Explain, mechanically in terms of gradient updates, why a mislabeled training example actively pushes weights toward the wrong behavior rather than merely failing to help.
Explain the quality-over-quantity principle and why the review bar must scale with dataset size rather than staying fixed.
Identify dataset problems that survive per-example correctness checks: duplication, distribution mismatch with production traffic, and missing coverage of edge cases or minority classes.
Design a dataset preparation checklist -- deduplication, format validation, label-balance checks, and a held-out validation split -- and explain what failure mode each step catches.

sections.heading: Format Fidelity: Train the Way You'll Serve
sections.body:
A fine-tuning dataset teaches the model a mapping: 'given input shaped like this, produce output shaped like that.' That mapping is only useful if the 'input shaped like this' half matches what real production requests look like. If your training examples are bare user messages with no system prompt, retrieved context, or conversation history, but production requests always include all three, the model was trained on inputs that don't match what it will be asked to handle, and there's no guarantee that what it learned from the clean, minimal format transfers to the messier, fuller real request. Most fine-tuning APIs expect examples in the same chat message format you'll serve with (system, user, assistant turns), which makes matching the format easier.

It sounds obvious, yet it's a common failure because training data is often assembled separately, sometimes by a different team or pipeline, from the code that builds production requests. The two drift apart unnoticed until the fine-tuned model in production looks weaker than it did in evaluation on the training format. The fix is boring but effective: generate training examples with the same request-building code path used in production (or a faithfully maintained copy), not a hand-rolled, simplified version that's easier to write by hand.

sections.heading: Why Bad Examples Hurt, Not Just Fail to Help
sections.body:
It's tempting to think of a mislabeled training example as 'wasted,' a data point that dilutes the dataset slightly but is otherwise harmless, like a blank line in a sum. That's not what happens. Every example produces a gradient telling the optimizer, with a direction and magnitude, to nudge weights toward giving higher probability to that example's target completion given its input. Gradient descent has no notion of 'this example is unreliable, weight it less' unless you build that in; by default every labeled example is trusted equally.

So a mislabeled example (a review that's negative but labeled positive, a ticket that's urgent but labeled routine) doesn't sit inertly; it teaches the model 'for input like this, the right response looks like that,' where 'that' is wrong. An isolated error among many correct examples has a small gradient signal relative to everything else, and its net effect may be negligible. But if a meaningful fraction of the dataset shares a *systematic* labeling error (the same annotator consistently mislabeling one category, a labeling script with a consistent bug), that isn't noise that averages out; it's a consistent, repeated signal, exactly what gradient descent learns well, pointed at the wrong target. A dataset needn't be mostly wrong to do damage: a correlated error affecting a modest fraction can bias the fine-tuned behavior in that direction. When labels come from an LLM or a script rather than people, audit that source the same way: a consistent quirk in the labeler becomes a consistent quirk in your model.

sections.heading: Quality vs Quantity
sections.body:
None of this means more data is bad; more correct, representative data is almost always better. But more data isn't free: it takes time to review, costs more compute to train on, and, if review effort doesn't scale with volume, growing the dataset grows the absolute number of unreviewed, possibly wrong examples even if the *rate* of errors stays constant. Ten thousand automatically-scraped examples with an unexamined 5% error rate contain about five hundred actively-wrong training signals; a hand-reviewed set of one thousand examples with a verified near-zero error rate contains close to none.

Practical experience supports this: for a narrow, well-specified behavior shift, a few hundred to a few thousand carefully verified examples often outperforms tens of thousands of unreviewed ones. There's no universal number for 'enough data'; it's task-dependent and found empirically. But the review bar has to scale with the data you add. Treating 'more data' and 'more review effort' as separable decisions is how a dataset accumulates enough bad signal to hurt the fine-tune while looking like an impressively large training set.

sections.heading: Coverage and Distribution Match: Clean Isn't Representative
sections.body:
A dataset can pass every per-example accuracy check (every label correct, every example well formed) and still be a poor training set if its overall distribution doesn't match production. It's the problem covered for few-shot examples in the prompting module (a classifier shown only positive and neutral examples has no demonstrated precedent for negative), baked in through weight updates instead of one prompt: if your examples are overwhelmingly short and simple while production traffic is long and complicated, or overwhelmingly one tone or language while traffic is more varied, the fine-tune will reproduce the narrow slice the training distribution showed and handle everything else with no precedent to draw on.

The reliable way to catch this is to hold out a validation split that you don't train on and measure performance on it. A random slice of the same possibly skewed dataset catches memorization but not distribution mismatch, so ideally sample the validation set independently from something closer to real production traffic. Training loss alone, measured on the training set, can keep decreasing while the model memorizes quirks of the training examples instead of learning behavior that generalizes to the inputs it will see. A steadily dropping training loss is consistent with genuine learning and with pure memorization alike; a held-out validation set drawn from a representative distribution is what tells them apart.

sections.heading: A Practical Preparation Checklist
sections.body: In practice: **deduplicate** near-identical examples before training, since duplicates add no new signal, only inflate the weight of whatever pattern they share and can push the model to overfit one overrepresented case. **Verify format** matches the real production request shape, not a simplified hand-built approximation. **Human-review a random sample** of the dataset, not the first ten examples someone looked at while building it, since early examples are often the most carefully constructed and least representative of what crept in later. **Check label and category balance**, and verify that minority classes and edge cases are present in numbers large enough to matter. **Hold out a validation split** drawn from a distribution that matches real traffic, and track validation performance, not just training loss, across the run. Split by source (by ticket thread, by customer, by document) rather than by individual example, so near-copies of a training example can't leak into validation and flatter the score. **Scrub sensitive data** (personal information, credentials, text you don't have the right to train on) before it is baked into weights, where it can't be selectively removed later. Start with a small pilot of a few dozen to a hundred examples to confirm the format and pipeline work before investing in a large dataset. After training, **re-run the broad regression evaluation** from the previous concept, since a dataset-quality problem and catastrophic forgetting can produce similar symptoms (the model getting worse at things it handled before) for different reasons, and telling them apart usually starts with re-examining what the training data contained.

examples.title: Format Mismatch Between Training Data and Real Requests
examples.explanation: The training example is a bare prompt/completion pair with no system message, retrieved context, or conversation history, convenient to write by hand in bulk but nothing like what `build_production_request` sends at inference time, which wraps the question in a longer structure with grounding instructions and injected context. A model fine-tuned only on the bare format learned a mapping from an input it will almost never see in production. The reverse mismatch happens too: a model trained with a long system prompt in every example learns to expect it, and may behave differently when the prompt is later shortened or edited, so treat the prompt as part of the trained artifact. It may still perform reasonably, since language models often generalize across superficial formatting differences, but that's not guaranteed; the safer approach is generating training examples through the same request-construction function used in production. (`SYSTEM_PROMPT_WITH_GROUNDING_INSTRUCTIONS` is a placeholder for your own system prompt.)

examples.title: One Systematically Mislabeled Category Among Many Correct Ones
examples.code:
dataset = [
    {"text": "Loved this, exceeded expectations!", "label": "positive"},        # correct
    {"text": "Terrible, broke after one day.", "label": "negative"},           # correct
    {"text": "It's okay, does the job.", "label": "neutral"},                  # correct
    {"text": "Waste of money, do not buy.", "label": "neutral"},               # WRONG: actually negative
    {"text": "Completely useless, regret this purchase.", "label": "neutral"}, # WRONG: same systematic error
    {"text": "Great value, works perfectly.", "label": "positive"},           # correct
]

# Suppose this "neutral for clearly negative" mislabeling pattern came from one
# annotator's consistent misunderstanding of the labeling guidelines, and
# affects roughly 20% of the negative-review examples across the full dataset.
examples.explanation: Two of the six examples shown are mislabeled, and they aren't random: they share the same systematic error, clearly negative reviews labeled neutral. A single isolated mislabel among hundreds of correct examples contributes a small, likely overwhelmed gradient signal. A *systematic* pattern like this, affecting a consistent fifth of a category across the dataset, is a repeated, correlated signal, the kind of regularity gradient descent picks up well, pointed the wrong way. The realistic consequence isn't a model that is unreliable everywhere; it's one biased toward labeling negative sentiment neutral, roughly in proportion to how often the error appeared in training, a subtle, specific bias that a spot-check of the first few examples would likely miss.

examples.title: A Dataset Validation Report Before Training
examples.code:
from collections import Counter

def validate_dataset(examples, expected_format_keys, min_label_fraction=0.05):
    report = {}

    seen_texts = [ex.get("prompt", "") for ex in examples]
    report["duplicate_count"] = len(seen_texts) - len(set(seen_texts))

    report["malformed_examples"] = [
        i for i, ex in enumerate(examples) if not expected_format_keys.issubset(ex.keys())
    ]

    label_counts = Counter(ex.get("label") for ex in examples if "label" in ex)
    total = sum(label_counts.values())
    if total:
        report["underrepresented_labels"] = [
            label for label, count in label_counts.items()
            if (count / total) < min_label_fraction
        ]

    lengths = [len(ex.get("prompt", "")) for ex in examples]
    report["length_range"] = (min(lengths), max(lengths)) if lengths else (0, 0)

    return report

dataset = [
    {"prompt": "Where is my order?", "completion": "Let me check that for you.", "label": "shipping"},
    {"prompt": "Where is my order?", "completion": "I'll look into it.", "label": "shipping"},   # duplicate prompt
    {"prompt": "Cancel my plan.", "completion": "Done, it ends this month.", "label": "billing"},
    {"prompt": "Reset my password", "label": "account"},   # malformed: no completion
]

report = validate_dataset(
    examples=dataset,
    expected_format_keys={"prompt", "completion"},
    min_label_fraction=0.30,
)
print(report)
# {'duplicate_count': 1, 'malformed_examples': [3], 'underrepresented_labels': ['billing', 'account'], 'length_range': (15, 18)}
examples.explanation: Each check targets a specific failure mode from the explanation, not a vague notion of 'data quality.' `duplicate_count` catches duplicates that would inflate one pattern's weight (this version catches exact duplicate prompts; near-duplicates need fuzzy matching or embeddings). `malformed_examples` catches examples missing required fields, which would fail or misbehave partway through a training run. `underrepresented_labels` catches classes so thin that the fine-tune has little precedent to learn a boundary from, the coverage problem from the prompting module, now checked at preparation time. `length_range` is a cheap first signal for distribution mismatch: if production requests run to several hundred characters and this range tops out at sixty, the training distribution probably doesn't match real traffic. The sample data here is made up so the report is runnable; the comment shows the output.

misconceptions.description: More training examples is always better, regardless of how carefully they were reviewed -- a bigger dataset can only help, or at worst just be somewhat inefficient.
misconceptions.clarification: Every training example produces a gradient signal that the optimizer trusts equally by default, so a mislabeled or unrepresentative example doesn't sit inertly diluting the dataset; it pushes weights toward the wrong association with the same confidence as a correct example. Growing a dataset without growing the review effort grows the absolute number of wrong signals even if the error rate stays constant, and a smaller, verified dataset often outperforms a much larger, less-reviewed one for this reason.

misconceptions.description: As long as training loss is steadily decreasing during a fine-tuning run, the model is learning the intended behavior well.
misconceptions.clarification: A steadily decreasing training loss is consistent with generalizable learning, but equally with the model memorizing quirks of the training examples (their exact phrasing, their format, accidental patterns in how they were built) instead of the broader behavior you want. Only performance on a held-out validation split drawn from a distribution matching real usage can distinguish generalization from memorization; training loss, measured on the data the model is fit to, cannot.

exercises.prompt: This function builds a fine-tuning dataset from a support-ticket database, but the resulting fine-tune ends up giving the exact same canned-sounding response to a common ticket type, ignoring real variation in how those tickets are actually phrased. Find the bug in the dataset-building logic and fix it.
hints: This function takes tickets in whatever order the database returns them and stops at max_examples. If one common ticket category is heavily overrepresented near the start of that ordering, what ends up dominating the dataset?

Nothing here checks for near-duplicate (question, reply) pairs. If the same common issue produces hundreds of very similar tickets with similar canned replies, how many effectively identical examples might end up in the first 5000?

Consider deduplicating near-identical examples and/or capping how many examples any single ticket category can contribute, so the dataset doesn't end up dominated by whichever pattern happened to be most common in the raw ticket volume.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original function has no deduplication and no per-category cap: it takes tickets in database order until it hits `max_examples`, so if one common issue generates a disproportionate share of tickets (typical, since a handful of issue types dominate real support volume), that category can fill most of the dataset with near-identical question/reply pairs. Gradient descent doesn't count repeated near-duplicates as one signal; it applies the gradient from every example, so the overrepresented category's pattern is reinforced far more strongly than any other, producing the reported symptom: an inflexible, canned response to that ticket type and weak coverage of everything else. The fix adds a duplicate check (skip prompts already seen, which catches exact duplicates only) and a per-category cap, so category balance reflects a deliberate choice instead of the order and volume in which the data arrived. (A real pipeline would also shuffle before truncating.)

exercises.prompt: Write a function label_balance(examples, min_fraction) that takes a list of dicts each with a "label" key, and returns a dict with two keys: "counts" (a dict mapping each label to how many examples have it) and "underrepresented" (a list of labels whose share of the total is strictly below min_fraction). This is meant to catch classes that are technically present in a dataset but too thin to give the model real precedent to learn from.
hints: Count occurrences of each label first -- a dict or collections.Counter works well here.
A label's "fraction" is its count divided by the total number of examples, not divided by the number of distinct labels.
Compare each label's fraction against min_fraction using a strict less-than -- a label sitting exactly at the threshold should NOT be flagged as underrepresented.
exercises.solutionExplanation: This checks the coverage principle from the explanation: a class can be present (here 'negative' and 'neutral' both have examples) yet so thin relative to the whole that the fine-tune has little signal to learn its boundary from. Counting with `Counter` and dividing by the total gives each label's share of the dataset, the number that matters, since 5 examples might be plenty in a 20-example dataset but thin in a 10,000-example one. Strict `<` rather than `<=` means a label exactly at the threshold counts as acceptable, as the requirement states. Run a check like this before committing to a training run, so a skewed balance can be corrected (targeted collection, or upsampling) instead of discovered after the fine-tune underperforms on the thin classes.

assessments.prompt: A team is choosing between fine-tuning on 50,000 examples scraped automatically from old support logs with an estimated 8% mislabeling rate, or 2,000 examples that were individually hand-verified for correct labels. Which is more likely to produce a better fine-tune, and why?
options: They are roughly equivalent, since gradient descent naturally discounts a small minority of incorrect examples during training regardless of dataset size, and a larger set always produces a better result.
The 50,000-example set, because a larger validation split can always be carved out of it afterward to compensate for the mislabeling.
The 50,000-example set, because fine-tuning quality is primarily a function of dataset size, and a mislabeling rate under 10% is negligible at that scale.

The 2,000-example set, because mislabeled examples actively teach the wrong association rather than merely diluting the signal, and 8% of 50,000 is a large, systematic amount of actively-wrong training signal.
assessments.explanation: Gradient descent trusts every labeled example equally by default; nothing automatically discounts examples because they're a minority, which is what the “They are roughly equivalent, since gradient descent…” option wrongly assumes. 8% of 50,000 is 4,000 mislabeled training signals, each pushing weights toward an incorrect association with the same confidence as a correct one, which is a substantial source of wrong signal and contradicts the “The 50,000-example set, because fine-tuning quality…” option. The “The 50,000-example set, because a larger validation…” option misunderstands validation: carving a split out of the same noisy dataset doesn't remove the noisy training examples, and a split from an equally noisy source wouldn't reliably reveal the problem. The hand-verified set avoids this wrong signal almost entirely, which is why it's the stronger choice despite being 25 times smaller.

assessments.prompt: Explain, mechanically in terms of gradient updates, why a fine-tuning dataset with a nontrivial fraction of mislabeled examples doesn't just 'partially help' the fine-tune -- it can make the model measurably worse at the task than not fine-tuning at all. Also explain what role a held-out validation set plays in catching this before it ships.
assessments.modelAnswer: Every training example, correct or not, produces a gradient during backpropagation, a direction and magnitude the optimizer uses to nudge every trainable weight so the model gives higher probability to that example's target completion given its input. The optimizer can't tell a correctly labeled example from a mislabeled one; both are treated as trustworthy ground truth and produce a gradient applied with the same confidence. So a mislabeled example isn't neutral or 'wasted': it teaches the model that, for an input like this, the right response looks like the wrong target it was paired with. A single isolated mislabel among thousands of correct examples may have a negligible net effect. But a *systematic* fraction of mislabeled examples (the same kind of error repeated, as opposed to scattered independent noise) is a consistent, correlated signal that gradient descent learns well, pointed at the wrong target. Enough of it can outweigh the correct signal on exactly the inputs it affects, producing a model measurably worse on that slice than the untouched base model, because it was taught the wrong association instead of merely left un-improved. A held-out validation set, one that is itself verified as accurately labeled and drawn from a distribution matching real usage, catches this before deployment: it reveals the gap between 'looks good because the model was fit to this flawed data' and 'good at the underlying task,' a gap that watching training loss fall on the flawed set can't reveal, because training loss measures agreement with the flawed labels.

assessments.prompt: Per this module, why can a model fine-tuned exclusively on bare prompt/completion pairs (no system prompt, no retrieved context, no conversation history) underperform in production even if every individual training label is correctly written?
options: Fine-tuning APIs silently discard any training example that lacks an explicit system message before training begins.
Bare prompt/completion pairs always take substantially longer to tokenize, which measurably slows down the model's convergence during training.

The model was trained on a mapping from an input shape it will essentially never see in production, since real requests include a system prompt, injected context, and history -- and there's no guarantee that what it learned from the clean, minimal training format transfers cleanly to that messier, fuller real request shape.
Bare prompt/completion pairs are always rejected outright by fine-tuning APIs, so this scenario could not actually occur in practice.
assessments.explanation: Training data teaches a mapping from a specific input shape to a desired output shape, and if that shape doesn't match real requests, nothing guarantees the learned behavior transfers, even if every label is correct in isolation. The “Bare prompt/completion pairs are always rejected outright…” option invents an API restriction. The “Bare prompt/completion pairs always take substantially longer…” option blames tokenization speed, an unrelated concern. The “Fine-tuning APIs silently discard any training example…” option invents a silent-discard behavior.

assessments.prompt: Per this module, why can training loss keep decreasing steadily throughout a fine-tuning run even as the model increasingly just memorizes quirks specific to the training examples rather than learning behavior that generalizes?
options: Training loss is measured only against the training data itself, so by construction it cannot distinguish genuine generalization from memorization of that same data -- only a held-out validation split drawn from a representative distribution can reveal that difference.
Training loss always rises sharply the moment memorization begins, so a steadily decreasing loss is, by itself, proof that memorization is not occurring.
Training loss is effectively a random number generated independently of the model's actual weight values, so it carries no real information either way.
Memorization is mathematically impossible under gradient descent, so this described scenario could not actually happen in a real training run.
assessments.explanation: A steadily dropping training loss is consistent with genuine learning and with pure memorization alike, because it's measured only on the data the model is fit to, so a held-out validation split from a representative distribution is needed to tell them apart. The “Training loss is effectively a random number…” option calls training loss meaningless noise, ignoring its direct relationship to the model's fit on the training data. The “Training loss always rises sharply the moment…” option asserts the opposite of the point: decreasing loss is compatible with memorization. The “Memorization is mathematically impossible under gradient descent…” option denies a real, common risk.

assessments.prompt: A support-ticket training dataset is built by pulling examples in raw database order until a fixed example count is reached, with no deduplication and no per-category cap. Per this module, what's the likely consequence, and why?
options: This concern only applies to classification-style tasks and has no relevance to tasks involving generated free-text replies like support-ticket responses.

Whichever ticket category is most common in raw volume is likely to dominate the resulting dataset with many near-identical examples, and since gradient descent applies a gradient to every example rather than discounting repeated near-duplicates, that category's pattern gets disproportionately reinforced at the expense of others.
No real consequence -- database order has no bearing on dataset composition, since every ticket is equally likely to be included regardless of order.
The dataset will automatically balance itself, since fine-tuning APIs enforce a hard cap on how many similar examples can be drawn from any single source category.
assessments.explanation: An unordered pull with no dedup and no per-category cap tends to let the category most common in raw volume dominate the dataset, and since gradient descent doesn't count repeated near-duplicates as one signal, that category's pattern is reinforced far more strongly than others. The “No real consequence -- database order has…” option ignores that ticket categories are rarely uniformly distributed in raw order or volume. The “The dataset will automatically balance itself, since…” option invents a safeguard that fine-tuning APIs don't provide. The “This concern only applies to classification-style tasks…” option wrongly limits the concern to classification, when the example here is free-text support replies.
